claims.text: The initial composite contains tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten structures within a copper matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation and interfacial void formation, especially during thermal cycling and irradiation.
A conformal, nanometer-scale Ni coating should be applied to tungsten surfaces before composite consolidation.
Optimizing the Ni coating thickness will minimize additional interfacial thermal resistance.
The proposed processing requires vacuum or inert-atmosphere handling and thermal treatment at approximately 500–600 °C in a reducing environment.
The intended service environment combines high heat flux with neutron or ion irradiation relevant to plasma-facing and cooling-joint applications.
The intervention produces a thin, continuous Ni interlayer at the W/Cu interface.
The Ni interlayer improves wetting between tungsten and copper.
The Ni interlayer enhances W/Cu interfacial cohesion.
The Ni interlayer functions as a diffusion barrier that retards atomic migration.
Retarding atomic migration reduces phase separation at the W/Cu interface.
The Ni interlayer limits vacancy accumulation that would otherwise produce interfacial voids.
Ni has intermediate solubility that fosters a compositionally graded interface.
A Ni-mediated graded interface mitigates local thermal stresses during cycling and irradiation.
Compared with an untreated W–Cu composite, the optimized Ni-coated composite will exhibit less phase separation and fewer interfacial voids.
Compared with an untreated W–Cu composite, the optimized Ni-coated composite will have higher thermal conductivity under combined high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
Phase separation and interfacial void formation degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites under service conditions.
The intervention's efficacy depends on precise control of coating and processing conditions.
A Ni interlayer may introduce additional thermal resistance if it is too thick.
